http://www.jpost.com/history/article-905.text: Jürgen Stroop, the Nazi commander who led the killing of more than 50,000 Jews, was sitting in a cell in Warsaw awaiting his own execution. Before he met the gallows, Stroop described in unrepentant detail his ascent as a Nazi, his destruction of the Warsaw Ghetto and his daily prosecution of mass murder. He gave his account to Kazimierz Moczarski, the journalist, Polish resistance leader and veteran of the Warsaw Uprising who shared Stroop's cell in Mokotów Prison for 255 days in 1949.Though he is now remembered as a hero for fighting the Nazi occupation, Moczarski was villainized by Poland's postwar Communist regime, which viewed his resistance group as a threat to their monopoly on power.His unlikely imprisonment alongside a former Nazi officer he'd once tried to assassinate gave Moczarski the chance to document Stroop's confessions in an influential book, “Conversations with an Executioner.”This book, despite being censored for years by the Polish government, proved revelatory about the psychology and motivations behind Nazi ideology.Moczarski died without ever seeing the book properly publishedAfter decades of being translated into over 15 languages and adapted for the stage and screen, “Conversations with an Executioner” was published Tuesday for the first time in an uncensored English translation by Steerforth, an imprint of Pushkin Press. The book's champions say it's about time. “On the one hand, this book is a central historical source for this really important event in the modern history of the world,” Sean Casper Bye, the book's English translator, told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency. “And at the same time, it's one that has continually struggled to get fully into publication.”The book's revelations about Stroop, the rise of Nazism and the psychology of genocide is reaching English readers after a long deferral. Moczarski made many unsuccessful attempts to publish “Conversations with an Executioner” after his release, but found little interest from publishers in Communist Poland. The book did not align with Communist ideological narratives about the Holocaust, which deemphasized tragedy in favor of total victory over the Nazis. And the government's crackdown on Polish resistance members, which led to Moczarski's imprisonment with Stroop, remained a taboo subject.A serialized version of the book first appeared in the Polish magazine Odra from 1972 to 1974, and Moczarski died the following year at age 68. He never saw the first censored edition in 1977, which removed references to the reasons behind his own incarceration. Nor did he see the publication of “Conversations with an Executioner” as an uncensored book in 1992, after the fall of Communism, when it became a bestseller. Now, the book has “canonical status” in Poland, said Bye. It has been included for years on required school reading lists, shaping how generations of Polish people remember the Holocaust.Moczarski's account also faced an uphill battle to reach English readers. During the Cold War, censorship, disrupted communication and closed archives in Eastern Europe made it difficult to publish books from Poland in English, said Bye. That lowered the focus on Eastern European sources and languages for years in Holocaust scholarship across English-speaking countries. The new English translation was championed by Clare Bullock, the book's editor in the United Kingdom, who has Polish Jewish heritage. She spent years pushing for it to appear in English at multiple publishing houses, said Bye. Moczarski and Stroop's fates were intertwined long before they shared a cell. During World War II, Moczarski joined the Home Army, the main Polish resistance force, where he worked for the Office of Information and Propaganda. Identifying local Nazi officials and collaborators as targets, Moczarski and his associates assassinated Stroop's predecessor, Franz Kutschera, nicknamed the “Butcher of Warsaw” for his mass executions of Polish civilians. They also made a failed attempt to kill Stroop, detailed by Moczarski in their cell. Though he was not Jewish, Moczarski supported and liaised with the Jewish Fighting Organization, known in Polish as ŻOB. The Home Army provided ŻOB leaders with weapons and technical instructions for the 1943 Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, the largest Jewish revolt against the Nazis. A year later, Moczarski fought in the Home Army's citywide Warsaw Uprising. The Nazis also brutally crushed this revolt, which led to the deaths of over 160,000 Poles, including some 17,000 Polish Jews who took part in the fighting or were discovered in hiding. Instead of being rewarded after the war, Moczarski was arrested in 1945 as the Communists consolidated their power in the aftermath of Nazi rule. The new regime baselessly declared the Home Army a quasi-fascist organization, claiming they had collaborated with the Nazis rather than fighting against them. Moczarski spent 11 years in prison, where, he would later recount, he endured 49 methods of torture. His confinement with Stroop made for another form of torture, according to Bye, who said it was “symbolically equating him, a brave Polish patriot, with a Nazi war criminal.” The men had a third cellmate: Gustav Schielke, a German former policeman turned low-ranking SS officer who resented the police's subordination to the Nazis, but did not resist them. In prison, these enemies lived under a code that required equality and confidentiality for survival. They slept on the floor together on three pallets, and Moczarski spent nights huddled between Stroop and Schielke to stay warm.Stroop opened up to Moczarski about the events of the ghetto uprisingMoczarski made it his mission to understand the war criminals. “If I succeed, I have the chance, if only to a certain extent, to answer my own question,” he wrote. “What historical, psychological, sociological mechanism led some Germans to come together into a gang of mass murderers who governed the Reich and did their utmost to introduce their 'Ordnung,' their Order, in Europe and the world?”He unraveled in Stroop an average German middle-class man of his time, with a low level of education, a drive to rise through military ranks, a reverence for order and obedience and a penchant for parroting Nazi ideology. As his defenses wore down, Stroop gave Moczarski a day-by-day account of his orders to crush the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising in 1943. Over nearly a month, his forces battled Jewish guerilla fighters and eventually burned down the ghetto block by block. He referred to the operations as “neutralizing” Jews or “cleansing” the Warsaw Ghetto of “subhumans.”When Moczarski asked Stroop whether he pitied the women fighters whom he captured and killed, he said the commander responded, after a long and “worked up” silence, with Nazi clichés. “Finally, the general straightens up, smooths down the hair at his temples and replies, in a chanting rhythm,” Moczarski wrote. “'Anyone wishing to be a true man in those days, meaning a strong one, had to act as I did. Gelobt sei was hart macht!'” The German phrase by Nietzsche, meaning “Praised be what hardens,” was taken from Nazi propaganda. In this portrait of Stroop, Bye saw a man who was motivated primarily by moving up the Nazi Party hierarchy. While Stroop repeated Nazi tropes and adapted his beliefs accordingly, upon becoming an SS officer, he broke with the Roman Catholic Church and declared himself “Gottgläubig,” a Nazi religious term, much of his testimony amounted to a boastful account of personal victories.“This was a type of Nazi,” said Bye. “Not everybody was a completely 100% committed idealogue. There were lots of people who were just ambitious and unscrupulous, and that was part of the engine that kept the Nazi machine going.” The idea that the Holocaust could have been willingly committed by everyday, career-minded people, not just Nazi ideologues and sadists, has been echoed in other landmark works of scholarship and culture, from Hannah Arendt's 1963 “Eichmann in Jerusalem” to the 2023 film “The Zone of Interest.” “Conversations with an Executioner” has been challenged as an authentic document, since Moczarski had no materials to take notes in the cell, yet recounted years of dialogue in vivid detail. Moczarski claimed that he honed an exceptional memory in prison and could write the book in his mind. After being released in 1956, he verified facts by obtaining Stroop's reports from the Polish Commission for Researching Nazi War Crimes and information from the US Pentagon archives.The limitations of the book as a firsthand account also make it a precious resource, said Bye. Stroop's destruction of the Warsaw Ghetto was so effective that “Conversations with an Executioner” provided a rare surviving window into what occurred.Bye said that voices like Moczarski's are becoming ever more crucial as the last generation of survivors die out and the Holocaust fades from living memory. He hopes the new English translation will give readers a counterweight to current-day narratives about the Holocaust, emerging in politics and elsewhere, that mold the past to fit ideological messages. “There are so many people who have a vested interest in getting us to look at the Holocaust in a particular way, who want to instrumentalize the Holocaust as this hugely emotionally weighty event for their own purposes,” he said.“One of the ways that we can keep in touch with the reality of the Holocaust is by going back to primary sources like this, going back to the people who did see it with their own eyes and who wrote about it themselves.”

https://scroll.in/latest/1095269/punjab-.text: Ad 1 HC summons journalist Sudhir Chaudhary for allegedly defamatory show during youth protests 2 How an anti-reservation movement mimicking the CJP is branding entitlement as reform 3 ‘Enough is enough’: Calcutta HC says it may bar more FIRs against Abhishek Banerjee 4 Why an indigenous community in Arunachal blacklisted four researchers 5 More Indian students are abandoning higher education as degrees no longer seem worth the cost 6 For children: Amal goes to the gurudwara kitchen with his grandmother when the langar is cooked 7 Ramachandra Guha: For 120 years, Indian students have fought to change politics and public life 8 Bombay HC refuses to quash defamation case against Rahul Gandhi for ‘choron ke sardar’ comment 9 Eiffel Tower shut as staffers protest women being removed for Hindu group’s visit 10 What Shrilal Shukla’s novel ‘Raag Darbari’ says about public administration, development, politics Former Indian diplomat Ramesh Chander | Ramesh Chander/LinkedIn Former Indian diplomat Ramesh Chander has been asked by the authorities conducting the special intensive revision of electoral rolls in Punjab to submit documents proving his citizenship , The Tribune reported on Tuesday. The 75-year-old told the newspaper that he has been “summoned to appear with proof of residence” at a government office on Thursday despite sharing his Aadhaar and voter identity cards with a booth level officer in Jalandhar. Chander told The Tribune that he has voted from Jalandhar in several elections, including the last Assembly elections in 2022 and the Lok Sabha polls in 2024. Chander served as India’s ambassador to Belarus and the consul general in Edinburgh, United Kingdom. He also held positions including India’s counsellor in Japan and a minister at the embassy in Prague, Czech Republic. He retired from the foreign service in December 2010. A notice issued to Chander by the additional electoral registration officer of Jalandhar West on Saturday said that the documents he submitted were insufficient to establish his eligibility as a voter, the newspaper reported. It also said that his voter details did not match those in the electoral roll used before SIR. Jalandhar Deputy Commissioner Varjeet Walia described the notice as part of the routine verification process, The Tribune reported. “Two categories of voters have so far been left out, those who are unmapped or those with logical discrepancies,” the newspaper quoted Walia as saying. He added that, under general instructions issued to booth level officers to make the process easier, Chander’s required documents would be collected from his home and he would not have to visit any office. On Sunday, retired diplomat Navdeep Suri also raised concerns about the verification process under the special intensive revision in Punjab. In a social media post, Suri said that he had to submit his Aadhaar and voter identity cards to a booth level officer and “was assured that everything is in order”. Suri said that he was later informed that some of his details did not match the electoral rolls from 2003, which are being used to verify voters during the exercise. Punjab is among the 16 states where the voter roll revision is being carried out in the third phase of SIR. In 2025, the first phase of the exercise was conducted in Bihar. It was extended to 12 states and Union Territories in the second phase in late 2025 and the first half of 2026. Since it began, concerns have been raised that the revision could eliminate genuine voters from the rolls and even shape electoral outcomes , as Scroll has reported. In May, the Supreme Court upheld the legality of the revision, but said that the exercise does not mean that the Election Commission can decide on whether the person is an Indian citizen. https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: The Thirlwall inquiry was launched in 2023 to examine events at the Countess of Chester hospital in Cheshire. Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty Images View image in fullscreen The Thirlwall inquiry was launched in 2023 to examine events at the Countess of Chester hospital in Cheshire. Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty Images Lucy Letby Analysis Thirlwall inquiry has left biggest questions around the Letby case unanswered David Conn Decision not to pause proceedings means £18m report does not engage with concerns over former nurse’s conviction Tue 15 Sep 2026 14.37 EDT Last modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 15.21 EDT Share Just two months before Lady Justice Kathryn Thirlwall opened her inquiry into events at the Countess of Chester hospital and the crimes of Lucy Letby, a report by Chris Henley KC was published into the “atrocious” wrongful conviction of Andrew Malkinson for rape. Henley prefaced that report with a plea for the legal establishment to recognise that the criminal courts produce miscarriages of justice. Right up to top judges in the court of appeal, Henley wrote, the system has “a deep-seated … cultural reluctance” to accept it “will on occasion make mistakes” and that “entirely innocent defendants will sometimes be convicted”. He said the system needed a culture that acknowledges mistakes can be made and ensures “in our various roles when making decisions we are all alive to this potential risk”. The Thirlwall inquiry was set up in 2023 by the then health secretary, Steve Barclay, on the basis that Letby was guilty of murdering seven babies, and attempting to murder seven more, at the Countess of Chester hospital’s neonatal unit where she was a nurse. Thirlwall’s terms of reference were to spotlight the hospital’s management, and whether their actions and culture “contributed to the failure to protect babies from Lucy Letby”. View image in fullscreen Lady Justice Kathryn Thirlwall arrives at Liverpool town hall before the publication of her inquiry report on Tuesday. Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty Images Many distinguished experts had already looked at the evidence and expressed very serious concerns that the system had made another of its mistakes and convicted an entirely innocent person. As the Guardian reported , 24 experts wrote to Wes Streeting, who took over as health secretary after Labour’s general election win in 2024, urging him to pause the inquiry or widen its terms of reference to examine the possibility of a miscarriage of justice. Streeting did not do so. In her opening speech in September 2024, Thirlwall, a court of appeal judge, referred to the criticisms of Letby’s convictions dismissively, referring to “a huge outpouring of comment” since the court of appeal refused Letby leave to appeal in May 2024, and to “all of this noise” that had caused distress to the bereaved parents. “It’s not for me to set about reviewing the convictions,” she said. “The court of appeal has done that with a very clear result. The convictions stand.” The core premise of the inquiry from the start was that the hospital’s managers had not acted on warnings about Letby from the consultants, and should have called in the police earlier. That was the central conclusion Thirlwall has reached in her 822-page report. She criticised “a prolonged delay by senior managers in calling the police” after the triplets, babies O and P at the trial, died in June 2016. There was an assumption throughout that the police, the Cheshire constabulary, were uniquely equipped to find the forensic truth about how the babies died. Thirlwall again emphasised in her final statement that her inquiry was “not an investigation into the criminal convictions or the guilt of Letby”. But the report is based on it being a fact that Letby is guilty and Thirlwall has delivered the devastating conclusion that babies would have been protected if the hospital had acted more quickly to safeguard them from the nurse. There was almost no moment in any of the gruelling inquiry sessions in the long, glittering ballroom of Liverpool town hall that engaged with the question looming over the proceedings: whether Cheshire constabulary may have got the case catastrophically wrong. A large group of British and international experts, led by the renowned Canadian neonatologist Dr Shoo Lee, who has argued relentlessly that his own research was misrepresented by the prosecution, concluded that there were no murders , only vulnerable newborn and premature babies, and poor care on the unit. View image in fullscreen From left to right: Letby’s barrister Mark McDonald, the Conservative MP David Davis and Dr Shoo Lee at a press conference in 2025. Photograph: Andy Rain/EPA Thirlwall heard in exhaustive detail about the actions the medical director, Ian Harvey, his management colleagues and the consultants took when considering the deaths and collapses of the babies. Postmortems had been carried out by three very experienced consultant pathologists at Alder Hey, Liverpool’s renowned children’s teaching hospital. They found no deliberate harm or any suspicion of it. Harvey had asked the Alder Hey pathologists to review their conclusions and they confirmed their original findings. He also had the babies’ deaths reviewed by a consultant neonatologist, Dr Jane Hawdon, of London’s Royal Free hospital. She also did not find any deliberate harm, but identified many areas of “sub-optimal care” on the unit. The Guardian view on Lucy Letby: Thirlwall should have waited for the pending case review | Editorial Read more Harvey invited a review by the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health, whose team came to a conclusion grimly familiar to maternity and children’s units in the NHS around the country. It had insufficient consultants and not enough consultant time was being spent on babies of such medical vulnerability, just two ward rounds each week. The management downgraded the unit so that it would no longer care for babies born so prematurely. Thirlwall examined all those processes and has concluded that none were adequate. Her conclusions are that when the consultants had raised concerns about Letby, safeguarding should immediately have been introduced and the police should have been called in earlier. So during two years and £18m spent on so much legal inquiry, the question has not been answered, nor was it allowed to be asked: how and why did Cheshire constabulary and the Crown Prosecution Service, and the doctors they recruited as expert witnesses, come to so wholly different a conclusion about the causes of death, from all the experts that had looked at the same medical evidence before? And nor was there permitted to be any solid engagement with the new experts, led by Lee, as to why they so fundamentally disagree with the prosecution’s case and convictions. In his call for more vigilance after the Malkinson catastrophe, Henley wrote: “Miscarriages of justice disfigure the lives of all connected to the case and make the public generally less safe.” The Criminal Cases Review Commission , the strained body whose role is to refer potential miscarriages of justice back to the court of appeal, is still looking at Letby’s application, and the copious expert reports submitted with it. In the meantime, a public inquiry chaired by a senior judge was set from beginning to end not to consider the possibility that the police, CPS and courts might have made a mistake, and served up a terrible injustice. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: Christa Pike entering a Knox county criminal court in Knoxville, Tennessee, on 4 December 2007. Photograph: J Miles Cary/Reuters View image in fullscreen Christa Pike entering a Knox county criminal court in Knoxville, Tennessee, on 4 December 2007. Photograph: J Miles Cary/Reuters Tennessee Tennessee halts plan to execute woman for first time in 200 years State governor and supreme court earlier refused calls for clemency for Christa Pike, who was convicted of murder Guardian staff and agency Wed 30 Sep 2026 12.26 EDT First published on Wed 30 Sep 2026 10.25 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Tennessee ’s first execution of a woman in 200 years was halted by a court on Wednesday morning an hour before it was set to take place . The state governor and the supreme court had earlier refused calls for clemency in the case of Christa Pike , who was convicted of murder 30 years ago. She was set to die by lethal injection at 11am ET on Wednesday but the execution has been halted by a federal appeals court. In a 2-1 majority, the court said: “The interests of justice and the finality of Pike’s impending execution compel the entry of a short stay of execution in order to properly analyze the parties’ fully briefed arguments and resolve the issues on the merits.” Stephen Ferrell, Pike’s attorney, said: “The court has stayed this recognizing the serious concerns about Christa’s scheduled execution.” The office of Jonathan Skrmetti, the state attorney general, issued a statement reacting to the news on Wednesday, saying: “We will continue to advocate for the lawfully imposed sentence as the courts work through this technical issue. It is common in capital cases for the defense to raise last-minute objections following decades of litigation in numerous courts. We are asking the supreme court of the United States to lift the stay.” The American Civil Liberties Union, which has opposed Pike’s execution, issued a statement on Wednesday, saying: “Hours before Tennessee was set to execute the first woman in the state in more than 200 years today, a federal court temporarily paused Christa Pike’s execution. Tell Governor Lee to respect the court’s decision and call off her execution now.” The Guardian has reached out to the office of Bill Lee, Tennessee’s Republican governor. Ahead of Pike’s scheduled execution, Lee declined to intervene, saying on Tuesday: “After deliberate consideration of Christa Gail Pike’s request for clemency and after a thorough review of the case, I am upholding the sentence of the state of Tennessee and do not plan to intervene.” Pike, who is now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend, who was 17 at the time, killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, one of their classmates at Knoxville Job Corps in 1995. The case garnered nationwide headlines due to the ages of those involved and the brutality of the murder. According to prosecutors, Pike was worried that Slemmer was trying to take her then boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, away fom her. Together, they lured Slemmer into a wooded area behind the agriculture campus steam plant at the University of Tennessee on 12 January 1995. Pike then cut Slemmer’s stomach and throat with a box cutter before smashing her head with a rock. Shipp carved a pentagram into Slemmer’s chest and Pike later showed a friend a fragment of Slemmer’s skull. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Around 2-3 times a day Sign up to Breaking News US Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion Shipp was convicted of first-degree murder in 1997 and was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole. Pike has never denied her involvement in Slemmer’s killing and was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder. “I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid. It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done. Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime,” Pike said in a statement that was included in her clemency petition. On Saturday, May Martinez, Slemmer’s mother, said she was waiting for Pike’s execution. “Every time I think about it, I think about Colleen feeling that pain and trying to get up and run,” Martinez told the Associated Press, adding: “Not a day goes by, or a minute goes by that I do not think about Colleen. Holidays are the worst.” The Associated Press contributed reporting. https://www.politico.eu/article/emmanuel.text: BRUSSELS — French president Emmanuel Macron warned fellow EU leaders they need to get a deal on the bloc's seven-year budget by the end of the year because it'll be too politically difficult after that, four European diplomats said. His words rachet up the pressure on the EU to overcome their significant differences over the coming weeks. During a closed-door discussion on Thursday evening, Macron said he wouldn't have a political mandate to sign a deal close to the French presidential elections in April 2027, the diplomats, all briefed on the conversation, said. Advertisement Advertisement Macron "said that, starting from January, there will be no political room" for concluding an agreement, one of the diplomats said. The EU’s 27 governments are divided over the total size of the 2028-2034 budget. Leaders gathering in Brussels are discussing the Irish plan , which envisions cuts of €159 billion in current prices to the Commission’s nearly €2 trillion proposal. European Council President António Costa is pushing leaders to finalize negotiations during a summit in December — before elections in France, Italy and Poland in 2027 threaten to derail the talks — but some governments and EU officials have said such a timeframe is very unrealistic. One EU diplomat dismissed Macron’s intervention as “a threat to support [Costa] on December deadline. “EU would be ungovernable if we were to take into account all the local elections,” he added. French far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who is leading the polls to replace Macron, pledged to halve France’s contributions to the EU budget if she comes to power. During a press conference in Brussels on Wednesday, Le Pen accused the EU of speeding up talks to prevent France's next leader to have a say. Several leaders are unwilling to commit to the end-of-year deadline, fearing that time pressure will undermine their leverage in the negotiations. “We will not sign an agreement that is not beneficial to us just to meet a deadline,” Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni told the country's parliament on Wednesday. “We will sign an agreement only when it is right for Italy.” Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Rescue workers at the site of Wednesday’s rail disaster in Spain’s Toledo province. A high-speed service hit another train halted by a signalling fault. Photograph: Burak Akbulut/Anadolu/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Rescue workers at the site of Wednesday’s rail disaster in Spain’s Toledo province. A high-speed service hit another train halted by a signalling fault. Photograph: Burak Akbulut/Anadolu/Getty Images Train crashes Analysis Second fatal train collision this year casts doubt over Spain’s high-speed rail network Ashifa Kassam in Madrid Questions were raised before Toledo crash over rail safety in a country where train travel has surged by 40% Deadly Spanish rail collision – latest updates Wed 28 Oct 2026 12.56 EDT First published on Wed 28 Oct 2026 10.29 EDT Share Spain’s high-speed rail network, the most extensive in Europe and the second largest in the world after China, has long been a point of pride in the country. But Wednesday’s deadly crash – the second in nine months – has recast the spotlight on questions about safety. Officials said at least 68 people were killed on Wednesday morning after a high-speed train slammed into another that had stopped on the tracks, leading to the derailment of several carriages. The two trains were believed to be carrying 544 passengers. Speaking to reporters, Spain’s transport minister, Óscar Puente, traced the collision back to a security system that had stopped working at about 8.30am local time. The computer malfunction brought an estimated six trains to a halt along a 63km stretch of track. Soon after, the central command in Madrid instructed one of the trains involved in the crash to resume service at normal speeds, sending it colliding into a train that was still sitting stationary on the tracks, said Puente. “It was the control centre – via its operators – that made the decision to resume operations, under circumstances that, from our point of view, are inexplicable,” he added . State-owned rail operator Renfe said in a statement that its train had been instructed to continue on its way and had crashed into ​the stationary Iryo train “for reasons we don’t know”. The accident follows a crash in January that killed 46 people and left dozens more injured near the town of Adamuz in Andalucía. View image in fullscreen A Guardia Civil officer collects evidence at the site of January’s fatal rail crash near Adamuz in Andalucía. Photograph: Manu Fernández/AP Media on Wednesday were swift to point to the parallels between the two crashes: both involved the same train operators and took place on the line connecting Madrid to the southern region of Andalusia, which is the oldest on Spain’s high-speed network. The first crash sparked conversation over safety on the line, a debate that rail unions say has continued. Wednesday’s disaster came a day before a planned 24-hour work stoppage at Renfe by Spain’s largest train drivers union. “Our goal is to change the system and make it safer,” the union said earlier this month. Their reasons for taking action ranged from the need for climate emergency protocols to ensuring channels of communication for workers to convey concerns. The union also called for guarantees that trains would be “reliable and safe”, adding: “We demand real and definitive technical solutions to the safety and reliability issues that have long plagued our rolling stock.” map It has also called a rolling, six-day strike for drivers at the high-speed rail operator Ouigo. The January crash sparked a bout of political finger-pointing over whether Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist party government had spent enough on railway maintenance in a country where travel by train accounts for about 57% of all transport. While the causes of the January crash remain under investigation, a preliminary report suggested that it could have been the result of defects in the track or in a weld between two sections of track. The report noted, however, that several other possibilities were also being investigated. Train travel grew by 40% from 2019 to 2024, coinciding with a period in which the country opened up its rail network to private companies. In the first half of this year, 25 million passengers used a high-speed train in Spain. The government says it has increased spending on railway network maintenance by 54% since taking power in 2018. View image in fullscreen The aftermath of the 2013 crash near Santiago de Compostela that claimed 80 lives. It remains Spain’s worst rail disaster. Photograph: Reuters Spain spends more than any other country on its high-speed network, averaging about €1.5bn (£1.26bn) a year from 2018 to 2022, according to a Reuters analysis of EU data. More than 90% of Spain’s train network is equipped with the highest level of safety control systems in the EU. Much of the funding, however, has seemingly been directed at new infrastructure, with about 16% earmarked for maintenance, renewal and upgrades. Data from the European Commission suggests Spain’s maintenance investment in its 4,000km (2,500 miles) of high-speed lines has lagged behind countries such as Germany or Switzerland although some of this could be attributed to differences in the age of the rail lines and the cost of public works and materials. Until this year, Spain had among the lowest accident rates in the EU, with just one or fewer fatalities per thousand kilometres of track, according to data from Eurostat, the statistics arm of the EU. On Wednesday, Spain’s prime minister said measures would be taken to rebuild trust in the country’s high-speed rail system. “Because it is simply unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed rail accidents in the same year, as we have,” said Sánchez. The crash was Spain’s worst rail accident since 2013, when 80 people died after a train veered off a curved section of track outside the north-western city of Santiago de Compostela. [AP Photo/Omar Havana] The EU summit held on Thursday and Friday in Brussels was an expression of the dangerous escalation of the international war crisis. While the Trump administration, amid its conflict with the European powers, is seeking at least for the moment a certain accommodation with Russia, the EU governments, led by Berlin, are pressing for the continuation and expansion of the Ukraine war. They want to shoulder an increasing share of the financial and military burdens themselves and build Europe into an independent military power. This is accompanied by an escalation that threatens to provoke a direct war between NATO and Russia, including nuclear war. At the same time, the summit discussions on rearmament, “competitiveness,” trade war and migration underscore that the war drive abroad is inseparably linked to intensified social attacks and authoritarian measures at home. Conflicts between Washington and Europe At the center of the summit was the demonstrative support for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. Following an agreement with Putin on Russian diesel supplies, Trump had eased sanctions and criticized Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries. He also demanded a change in Ukraine’s leadership. The European governments, by contrast, are determined to continue attacks on Russia’s energy infrastructure and tighten sanctions. European Council President António Costa declared on Friday, standing alongside Zelensky: “Now is not the time to withdraw support for Ukraine. Now is not the time to ease sanctions against Russia.” Instead, the EU must increase its support and pressure on Russia. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced preparations for a 22nd package of sanctions. The German government is taking a particularly aggressive stance. Chancellor Friedrich Merz declared that the EU must “once again ... increase” its funding for Kiev in order to “provide lasting support” to Ukraine. This was necessary, he said, to defend “the political order of Europe.” The conflict with Washington now also concerns control over approximately €210 billion in frozen Russian central bank assets in Europe. According to reports, US negotiators want to use part of these assets in negotiations with Moscow. Merz brusquely rejected this: “That is our affair, and we will decide on it.” Behind these differences lie rival geostrategic and economic interests. The European powers fear that Trump could conclude an agreement with Putin that would undermine their own war aims and influence in Eastern Europe. At the same time, Ukraine’s war effort remains dependent on American military technology and intelligence support. Reports of restrictions on the satellite-based Starshield system demonstrate this dependence particularly starkly. Ever more billions for war Zelensky put Ukraine’s war costs for 2027 at €155 billion and demanded at least €70 billion in additional European support. With this money, Ukraine could produce two to three times as many drones and massively increase military pressure on Russia. The EU has already set in motion a €90 billion loan for 2026 and 2027. No decision was reached in Brussels on the new demands for billions; the Commission has been tasked with developing financing options. The scale of the sums already mobilized is enormous. According to a study by the Kiel Institute for the World Economy, the German government puts its Ukraine support to date, including commitments, at around €100 billion. Approximately €41.7 billion is recorded as direct aid to Ukraine, while another €22 billion consists of future military commitments and possible expenditures. Together, this amounts to €63.7 billion, of which approximately €56.3 billion is military aid. In addition, €35.9 billion has been spent predominantly on Ukrainian refugees in Germany. Not all of the budgeted funds recorded have yet been disbursed. The political thrust of the Kiel study is revealing. Under a headline emphasizing that “only” €41.7 billion actually went to Ukraine, it stresses that spending on refugees does “not support the Ukrainian government in its defense.” This juxtaposition alone makes the political orientation clear: While support for refugees and other social expenditures face growing pressure for cuts, ever larger sums are to be mobilized for the war effort. Added to this are hundreds of billions more that are to flow into military budgets in the coming years. Concrete preparations for a NATO-Russia war Parallel to the summit, the military confrontation is intensifying. NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe Alexus Grynkewich presented his “Theory of Victory” in Warsaw: “Block, Blunt, Break.” A potential attack is first to be repelled, then the opposing armed forces smashed, and finally the command, supply and production structures supporting them disabled. Grynkewich describes the strategy as defensive, but in a major war the planned operations could extend deep into Russian territory. He praised Germany as the “engine of NATO.” At the same time, NATO conducted the nuclear war exercise “Steadfast Noon” in Italy this week, involving 17 countries, including German Tornado fighter jets. NATO describes it as a routine exercise without live nuclear weapons. Yet it rehearsed procedures for nuclear operations at a time when the risks of escalation are rapidly increasing. Russia is responding to NATO’s constant provocations with nuclear threats. In early October, Putin warned that Russia could use its entire arsenal in the event of a blockade of Kaliningrad. Now, State Duma Deputy Alexei Zhuravlyov has told Lenta.ru that, in the event of a NATO attack, Russian nuclear strikes could target NATO headquarters, as well as US nuclear weapons bases in Germany, Belgium, Italy and Turkey. Zhuravlyov’s threat is not an official government statement. His remarks nevertheless demonstrate how concretely sections of the Russian establishment are discussing nuclear war in Europe. Russian military commentators warn that NATO’s strategy could serve as a cover for “preemptive” strikes. They draw parallels to Hitler’s war of annihilation against the Soviet Union, which Nazi propaganda likewise justified as “defense” against an allegedly planned Soviet attack. Regardless of NATO’s specific timetable for war, the mutual threats already demonstrate that an escalation could rapidly spiral out of control. In the Black Sea, Romania and Bulgaria are demanding additional NATO measures against Russia following drone attacks on merchant ships. Ask more questions at SocialismAI.com Rearmament and social devastation Europe’s response to the war and the crisis of its alliance with Washington is a gigantic rearmament program. “ReArm Europe” is intended to make possible up to €800 billion in additional defense spending by 2030, while the SAFE program provides €150 billion in loans. In Germany, defense spending is to rise to approximately €140 billion in 2027—and to well over €200 billion in 2029. The German government wants to build the Bundeswehr into Europe’s strongest conventional army. These sums have immediate social consequences. While debt rules are relaxed for rearmament, European governments are organizing historic cuts to social benefits and public services. Under the slogan of “competitiveness,” the EU summit adopted measures for deregulation, accelerated approval procedures and further economic restructuring. Jobs are being eliminated on a massive scale, wages cut and working conditions worsened. The EU also wants to create new trade policy instruments to take tougher action, particularly against China. Merz stated that the Commission had been given a mandate to this end. Von der Leyen announced additional import restrictions. The migration debate at the summit also revealed its reactionary direction. Italy, Denmark and Poland attacked Spain’s planned legalization of the residence status of around 600,000 migrants. Discussions included tightening detention provisions in border procedures and suspending asylum applications in times of crisis. In the Middle East, against the backdrop of the US-Israeli war of aggression against Iran, the summit focused above all on securing trade and energy routes. As the EU advances its global war offensive and reactionary domestic agenda, tensions among the European imperialist powers are growing. The dispute over the next EU budget for 2028 to 2034 exposed these rivalries. Net contributors, such as Sweden, are refusing the higher contributions being demanded, while the EU seeks to mobilize additional funds for strategic and military projects. No agreement has yet been reached. The extreme escalation of war is also a response to growing social and political opposition in Europe. In France, Spain and other countries, mass protests and strikes are developing against social cuts, militarism and authoritarian measures. Confronted with the deep crisis of the established parties, the ruling classes are attempting to divert this opposition outward through war propaganda and nationalism and force the population to rally behind their war policies. But this course will only further intensify social antagonisms. The gigantic military expenditures, the destruction of jobs and social benefits, and the increasing attacks on democratic rights will not extinguish the resistance of the working class and youth but further fuel it. At the same time, the escalating confrontation with Russia threatens to plunge all of Europe into a nuclear world war. The decisive task is to arm the growing opposition with an independent socialist perspective. The working class must organize independently of the established parties and unite its struggles across all national borders against capitalism, militarism and war. The nationalist and militarist project of the European governments must be opposed with the struggle for the United Socialist States of Europe.
